introduction: The King of Navarre and three companions plan to win lasting fame through three years of study, fasting, little sleep, and avoidance of women. Berowne suspects that such ambitious rules will founder on ordinary human desire, especially with a French princess already expected on diplomatic business. Around their proposed academy, a boastful Spaniard, an agile page, country lovers, and learned word-spinners offer competing kinds of wit. Courtship soon makes promises and language much harder to control than the scholars expect.

fullSynopsis.text: Navarre persuades Berowne, Longaville, and Dumaine to sign the rules of his secluded academy. Berowne objects that fasting, sleeplessness, and abstinence from women are unreasonable, and reminds the king that the Princess of France must soon arrive to discuss Aquitaine. Necessity already requires an exception. Costard is punished for being found with Jaquenetta after Armado reports their meeting. Armado, however, confesses to his page Moth that he himself loves her, despite the vows he has made to study with the king. Moth's agile teasing punctures his master's elaborate self-importance.

The Princess arrives with Rosaline, Maria, and Katharine. Navarre receives the embassy outside the court because of his oath, leaving his guests in tents. Their business concerns disputed payments and the possession of Aquitaine; he promises to reconsider when documentary proof arrives. The ladies already know and praise the men who have sworn themselves scholars, while Berowne and Rosaline renew a sharp exchange of wit. After the meeting each lord seeks the name of a particular lady, and Boyet reads the king's behavior as unmistakable love for the Princess.

Armado frees Costard to carry a love letter to Jaquenetta. Berowne then employs the same messenger to deliver his own letter to Rosaline, accepting that he too has become a lover and oath-breaker. Costard exchanges the letters. The Princess's party receives Armado's extravagant address to Jaquenetta and makes sport of its inflated language. Jaquenetta, unable to read, takes Berowne's poem to Nathaniel and Holofernes. They identify its writer and intended recipient and send her to show it to the king as evidence that one of the sworn scholars has broken his undertaking.

Meanwhile Berowne secretly overhears Navarre, Longaville, and Dumaine reading love poems, each exposed after trying to hide and mock the next. Berowne finally steps out to denounce their hypocrisy, only to have his own letter arrive and betray him. With all four confessed, he supplies an argument for abandoning the vows: love is the true source of learning, courage, and artistic invention, and women's eyes are better academies than books. The men turn from concealment to a joint plan of courtship and entertainment. Armado and the local scholars prepare a pageant of the Nine Worthies.

Warned by Boyet that their suitors will arrive disguised as Russians, the ladies exchange the favors by which the men intend to recognize them. Their masked reception frustrates the men's speeches, dancing, and declarations, which are addressed to the wrong women. When the men return in their own identities, the ladies expose the trick and renew the mockery. Berowne vows to discard ornate language for plain speech. During the Nine Worthies show, however, the aristocratic audience persistently interrupts and humiliates the performers. Costard announces that Jaquenetta is pregnant by Armado, and a threatened fight adds to the disorder.

Marcadé arrives with news that the Princess's father is dead, abruptly ending the entertainment. Preparing to depart, she acknowledges that her diplomatic suit has been granted but refuses an immediate marriage. She requires Navarre to prove his constancy through a year of austere retirement while she mourns. Katharine and Maria also postpone their suitors' hopes. Rosaline requires Berowne to spend a year among the sick, testing whether his wit can comfort suffering instead of merely wounding easy targets. The men accept delay, without receiving the marriages a comedy might promise. Armado reports his vow to work Jaquenetta's plough for three years. Songs of spring and winter, with their cuckoo and owl, close the action amid pictures of courtship, married anxiety, labor, and ordinary seasonal life.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Navarre requires his three companions to sign an undertaking of three years' study, limited food and sleep, and avoidance of women. Berowne questions both its wisdom and its feasibility, particularly because the French Princess is coming on state business. He signs nonetheless, predicting that necessity will repeatedly undermine the oath. Dull brings Costard and an elaborate letter from Armado reporting his meeting with Jaquenetta. Costard's verbal evasions fail, and he is sentenced to fasting under Armado's custody. Armado then admits to Moth that he loves Jaquenetta himself. The page turns his master's grand phrases and borrowed heroic precedents into jokes. Armado declares his love to the countrywoman and resolves to express his passion in poetry, already anticipating his own perjury.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: The Princess sends Boyet to seek an audience and discusses Navarre's companions with her ladies. Maria praises Longaville, Katharine Dumaine, and Rosaline Berowne, giving their scholarly opponents a personal attraction before the encounter begins. Navarre welcomes the visitors but refuses them entry to the court, citing his vow. The Princess challenges the contradiction between courtesy and that exclusion. Their dispute over Aquitaine depends on whether French payments have been received; Boyet promises documentary proof the following day, and Navarre offers a renewed hearing. Berowne and Rosaline exchange quick challenges. The lords separately ask Boyet about their chosen ladies, while Boyet tells the Princess that Navarre's eyes and behavior have already disclosed his love.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Moth's song and account of fashionable wooing give Armado another occasion for extravagant speech and the page another opportunity to unsettle it. Armado orders Costard released from confinement so that he can serve as a messenger to Jaquenetta. After a chain of puns about riddles, endings, and Costard's injured shin, he supplies a letter and payment for the service. Berowne then meets Costard and gives him a second letter, addressed to Rosaline, with a larger reward. Alone, Berowne mocks the power Cupid has gained over a man who formerly mocked lovers. He recognizes both the loss of his independence and the breach of his oath, yet resolves to write, sigh, and pursue Rosaline.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Costard brings the Princess's party the wrong letter, so Armado's address to Jaquenetta is read aloud and ridiculed. Meanwhile Holofernes, Nathaniel, and Dull display rival kinds of learning through disputes about the hunted deer, Latin, and poetry. Jaquenetta asks them to read the other misdirected letter; they discover Berowne's love poem to Rosaline and send it to Navarre. In the park Berowne overhears the king, Longaville, and Dumaine successively reveal their love in verse while each hides from the next. He mocks them before Jaquenetta's arrival exposes him too. All four admit their broken vows. Berowne defends love as a richer education than secluded study, and the men agree to woo openly and devise entertainments for the ladies.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Armado recruits the local scholars and performers for the Nine Worthies. Boyet warns the women about the men's Russian disguises; exchanged favors cause the masked suitors to court the wrong partners. The ladies expose them on their return, and Berowne promises plain speech. The Worthies are then interrupted and mocked; Costard's announcement of Jaquenetta's pregnancy provokes Armado. News of the French king's death stops the show. The Princess leaves to mourn and requires a year's trial of Navarre's constancy. Her companions also defer marriage, with Rosaline assigning Berowne to comfort the sick and reform his mocking wit. Armado vows three years' labor for Jaquenetta. Contrasting songs of spring and winter close the play without carrying out the deferred marriages.
